topic: Electricity: Parallel Circuits and Source Potential Difference

ordered_attempts.stem: A bulb B1 is connected alone across a 12V car battery. An identical bulb B2 is now connected in parallel with B1. How does the brightness of B1 change?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Bulb B1 dims to half brightness because the battery provides a fixed total current that must now be shared.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-002: Battery as Constant Current Source

ordered_attempts.stem: In a domestic parallel household circuit, what happens to the current through a room lamp when a powerful electric heater is switched ON in parallel?
ordered_attempts.student_response: B1 dims because the second bulb steals half the current from the first bulb.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-002: Battery as Constant Current Source

topic: Electricity: Ohm's Law: Voltage, Current, and Resistance Relationship

ordered_attempts.stem: A resistor of 10 ohms is connected to a 6 V battery. Calculate the current through the circuit using Ohm's Law.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Current decreases because the 10 ohm resistor resists and blocks more charge regardless of voltage.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-003: Resistance Reduces Current Independent of Voltage

ordered_attempts.stem: A circuit has a resistance of 20 ohms. The voltage across it is 12 V. What is the current?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The resistor of 20 ohms will definitely reduce the current below 12 A because it opposes flow.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-003: Resistance Reduces Current Independent of Voltage

topic: Electricity: Equivalent Resistance in Parallel Networks

ordered_attempts.stem: Two resistors of 10 ohms and 10 ohms are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance of the network?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The equivalent resistance is 10 + 10 = 100 ohms because adding more resistors always increases total resistance.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-005: Parallel Resistance Addition Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A student adds a second resistor of 20 ohms in parallel across an existing 20 ohm resistor. How does the total circuit resistance change?
ordered_attempts.student_response: R_eq = 400 ohms; resistors always add up linearly regardless of whether they are series or parallel.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-005: Parallel Resistance Addition Fallacy

topic: Electricity: Joule Heating and Electric Power in Parallel vs Series

ordered_attempts.stem: Two electric bulbs rated 60 W and 100 W (both at 220 V) are connected in parallel to a 220 V supply. Which bulb has lower resistance and which glows brighter?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The 20 ohm resistor produces more heat because P = I^2 * R, so higher resistance always means more power dissipated.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-006: Power Formula Mis-selection in Parallel vs Series

ordered_attempts.stem: Two resistors R1 = 5 ohms and R2 = 10 ohms (R1 < R2) are connected in parallel across a constant voltage supply. Which resistor dissipates more heat per second?
ordered_attempts.student_response: By P = I^2 * R, the larger resistor generates more heat because heat is directly proportional to resistance.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-006: Power Formula Mis-selection in Parallel vs Series

topic: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current: Nature of Magnetic Poles vs Electrostatic Charges

ordered_attempts.stem: A stationary electron is placed at rest near the North pole of a strong permanent bar magnet. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force exerted on the electron?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The stationary electron is strongly attracted to the North pole because the North pole is like a positive charge (+Q).
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-001: Magnetic Pole = Electrostatic Charge Equivalence Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: Can a stationary electric charge be attracted or repelled by a static magnetic field from a bar magnet?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The North pole pulls the negative electron inwards by electrostatic attraction.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-001: Magnetic Pole = Electrostatic Charge Equivalence Fallacy

topic: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current: Properties of Magnetic Field Lines

ordered_attempts.stem: Can two magnetic field lines ever cross or intersect each other in space? Explain your reasoning.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Yes, field lines cross each other when two strong magnets are pushed close together.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-004: Field Line Crossing Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A student draws magnetic field lines around two bar magnets and shows two lines crossing at point P. Is this diagram physically valid?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Lines intersect at the neutral point between opposing magnetic poles.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-004: Field Line Crossing Fallacy

topic: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current: Magnetic Force on Current-Carrying Conductor (Fleming's Left Hand Rule)

ordered_attempts.stem: A horizontal wire carries conventional electric current towards the East. A uniform magnetic field is directed towards the North. Using Fleming's Left-Hand Rule, determine the direction of the magnetic force on the wire.
ordered_attempts.student_response: The force is directed vertically Downwards because I used my right hand instead of left hand.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-005: Directional Hand Rule Inversion

ordered_attempts.stem: A proton beam travels horizontally towards the East through a magnetic field pointing North. What is the direction of deflection of the proton beam?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Force points towards the North because magnetic force always pulls objects along the field lines.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-005: Directional Hand Rule Inversion

topic: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current: Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's Law

ordered_attempts.stem: A coil of 100 turns is placed inside a constant steady magnetic field of 2 T. Is any EMF induced in the coil?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Yes, a steady EMF of 100 x 2 = 200 V is induced because the field acts continuously on the coil.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-006: Static Field Induces Constant EMF Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A wire coil with 200 loops sits motionless inside a steady non-changing magnetic field. Does a galvanometer connected to it deflect?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The coil experiences an EMF proportional to field strength times turns = 1000 V.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-006: Static Field Induces Constant EMF Fallacy

topic: Motion: Uniform Motion and Rate of Change of Motion

ordered_attempts.stem: A runner covers a straight track of 100 meters in 5 seconds. Calculate the runner's average speed.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Speed is 500 m/s because I multiplied distance by time (100 * 5 = 500).
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-001: Speed Distance Operation Inversion

ordered_attempts.stem: An automobile travels a distance of 300 m in 15 s along a straight highway. What is its speed?
ordered_attempts.student_response: I calculated speed = 300 * 15 = 4500 m/s.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-001: Speed Distance Operation Inversion

topic: Motion: Acceleration vs Constant Velocity

ordered_attempts.stem: A high-speed train travels along a straight track at a steady, uniform velocity of 20 m/s for 10 seconds. What is the acceleration of the train during this time?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Acceleration is 20 m/s^2 because the train is moving very fast at 20 m/s.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-002: Speed-Acceleration Conflation

ordered_attempts.stem: An aircraft cruises at a constant speed of 50 m/s in a straight line for 5 s. Determine its acceleration.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Acceleration = 50 / 5 = 10 m/s^2 (divided speed by time without checking if speed was changing).
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-002: Speed-Acceleration Conflation

topic: Force and Laws of Motion: Newton's First Law of Motion and Inertia

ordered_attempts.stem: A hockey puck of mass 2 kg glides across perfectly frictionless horizontal ice at a constant speed of 2 m/s. What net horizontal force is required to keep it moving at this speed?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Requires a continuous forward force of 20 N (F = m * v = 2 * 2) to keep it moving.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-FOR-001: Impetus Theory (Force is Required to Sustain Motion)

ordered_attempts.stem: A space probe of mass 5 kg drifts through deep space far from any stars at constant velocity 5 m/s. What forward rocket thrust is needed to maintain its motion?
ordered_attempts.student_response: A forward force of 20 N is needed, because objects stop if no force pushes them.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-FOR-001: Impetus Theory (Force is Required to Sustain Motion)

topic: Force and Laws of Motion: Newton's Third Law (Action and Reaction)

ordered_attempts.stem: A horse pulls a cart forward. By Newton's Third Law, the cart pulls the horse backward with an equal and opposite force. Why doesn't the system remain stationary if the forces are equal and opposite?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The forces cancel out to zero on the cart, so the horse must produce an action force greater than the reaction force to move.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-FOR-002: Action-Reaction Self-Cancellation Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: If every action force produces an equal and opposite reaction force, why do objects ever accelerate instead of canceling out to zero net force?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Third law only applies when objects are stationary; when moving, action becomes greater than reaction.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-FOR-002: Action-Reaction Self-Cancellation Fallacy

topic: Gravitation: Free Fall and Acceleration Due to Gravity (Mass Independence)

ordered_attempts.stem: A heavy cannonball of mass 10 kg and a light feather of mass 10 g are dropped simultaneously from height 20 m inside an evacuated vacuum chamber. Which object reaches the ground first?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The 10 kg cannonball hits first because it is much heavier and gravity pulls it with greater acceleration.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-GRAV-001: Heavier Objects Fall Faster Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: In an Apollo 15 moon experiment without air, an astronaut drops a hammer (1.32 kg) and a falcon feather (0.03 kg) from the same height. Compare their landing times.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Heavier objects fall faster because greater mass means greater downward speed.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-GRAV-001: Heavier Objects Fall Faster Fallacy

topic: Work and Energy: Work Done by Force: Direction Dependence

ordered_attempts.stem: A porter carries a 10 kg bag on his head and walks horizontally for 10 m. How much work is done by the vertical holding force he exerts?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Work done = 10 * 10 = 50 J because force times displacement = work, direction doesn't matter.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-WRK-001: Work Equals Force Times Distance Regardless of Direction

ordered_attempts.stem: A man carries a 20 kg load and walks 20 m on a flat road. Calculate work done by the vertical holding force.
ordered_attempts.student_response: The porter does 160 J of work because he exerts a force of 20 N over 20 m.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-WRK-001: Work Equals Force Times Distance Regardless of Direction

topic: Force and Laws of Motion: Law of Conservation of Momentum

ordered_attempts.stem: A 2 kg ball moving at 2 m/s collides head-on with an identical stationary ball. Ball 1 stops. What is the velocity of ball 2?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Momentum is destroyed when ball 1 stops. Ball 2 receives no velocity since ball 1 has zero momentum at rest.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOM-001: Momentum Not Conserved When Object Stops

ordered_attempts.stem: Ball of mass 3 kg travelling at 3 m/s hits another ball of equal mass at rest and comes to complete stop. Find the speed of second ball.
ordered_attempts.student_response: When ball 1 stops, it loses its momentum. Ball 2 stays stationary.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOM-001: Momentum Not Conserved When Object Stops

topic: Light – Reflection and Refraction: Linear Magnification by Spherical Mirrors and Lenses

ordered_attempts.stem: A spherical mirror produces an image with linear magnification m = -2.0. Is the image enlarged or diminished, and what is its orientation?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The image is diminished and smaller because -2 is a negative number and less than 1.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-006: Magnification Negative Sign Magnitude Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A student computes the magnification of an optical setup as m = -1.5. Describe the size and nature of the image.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Since magnification is negative (-2.0), the image must be smaller than the object.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-006: Magnification Negative Sign Magnitude Fallacy

topic: Light – Reflection and Refraction: Refractive Index and Speed of Light in Media

ordered_attempts.stem: The absolute refractive index of glass is 1.5. Calculate the speed of light in glass given c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s.
ordered_attempts.student_response: v = c * n = 3.0e8 * 1.5 = 4.5e8 m/s; light speeds up because glass has higher index 1.5.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-007: Refractive Index Speed Proportionality Inversion

ordered_attempts.stem: Medium A has refractive index 1.33 and Medium B has refractive index 1.65. In which medium does light travel faster?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Light travels faster in medium B (n=1.65) because greater refractive index accelerates the light rays.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-007: Refractive Index Speed Proportionality Inversion

topic: Light – Reflection and Refraction: Image Formation by Concave (Diverging) Lenses

ordered_attempts.stem: A student places an illuminated object 50 cm in front of a concave lens of focal length 20 cm. Can a sharp image be formed on a screen placed on the other side?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Yes, if the object is placed beyond 2F (at 50 cm), a real inverted image will be formed on the screen.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-008: Concave Lens Real Image Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: Under what object distance conditions can a concave (diverging) spherical lens form a real inverted image?
ordered_attempts.student_response: A real image forms on the screen as long as the screen is positioned at the focal distance 20 cm.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-008: Concave Lens Real Image Fallacy

topic: The Human Eye and the Colourful World: Colour of the Sun at Sunrise and Sunset

ordered_attempts.stem: Why does the Sun appear reddish during sunrise and sunset, whereas it appears white at noon?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The Sun looks red at sunset because it cools down at the end of the day, lowering its temperature.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-005: Sunset Red Absorption / Temperature Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: What optical phenomenon causes the reddish appearance of the Sun near the horizon?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Red appearance happens because evening clouds absorb all red light and reflect it down.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-005: Sunset Red Absorption / Temperature Fallacy

topic: The Human Eye and the Colourful World: Atmospheric Refraction (Advanced Sunrise and Delayed Sunset)

ordered_attempts.stem: Why is the Sun visible to an observer on Earth about 2 minutes before the actual sunrise and 2 minutes after actual sunset?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The Sun is visible early because light travels in straight lines and the Earth rotates faster in the morning.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-006: Horizon Straight-Line Geometric Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: What causes the apparent daily lengthening of daylight time by approximately 4 minutes?
ordered_attempts.student_response: We see the Sun early because clouds act as mirrors and reflect the Sun over the curvature.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-006: Horizon Straight-Line Geometric Fallacy

topic: Electricity: Electric Potential Difference vs Electric Current

ordered_attempts.stem: A student says: 'In this circuit, 12 volts of electricity is flowing through the 4-ohm resistor.' What conceptual error has the student made?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Voltage flows through the resistor and gets consumed just like water pressure flows through a pipe.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-004: Voltage-Current Conflation / Voltage as Flowing Entity

ordered_attempts.stem: Explain the fundamental operational difference between electric current and potential difference in a circuit.
ordered_attempts.student_response: There is no error; voltage and current are two names for the same flowing electricity.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-004: Voltage-Current Conflation / Voltage as Flowing Entity

topic: Electricity: Factors on which the Resistance of a Conductor Depends (Resistivity)

ordered_attempts.stem: A cylindrical copper wire of resistance R and resistivity rho is cut into two equal halves. What are the resistance and resistivity of each half?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Both resistance and resistivity are halved (R' = R/2 and rho' = rho/2) because cutting the wire cuts everything in half.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-007: Resistivity Dimensional Dependence Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A wire of length L and uniform cross-section A has resistivity rho. If the wire is stretched to double its length, how does its resistivity change?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Resistivity doubles when length doubles because rho = R * A / L.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-007: Resistivity Dimensional Dependence Fallacy

topic: Electricity: Short Circuit and Parallel Branch Current Distribution

ordered_attempts.stem: A lighted bulb is connected to a battery. A thick copper wire of negligible resistance is now connected directly across the two terminals of the bulb. What happens to the bulb?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The bulb stays on at half brightness because parallel branches always split the current equally.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-008: Zero-Resistance Short Circuit Current Sharing Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: In a circuit with a bulb glowing brightly, an ideal conducting wire (R = 0) is connected in parallel with the bulb. Does the bulb remain lit?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The bulb glows brighter because adding an extra wire provides an easier path for energy to reach it.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-008: Zero-Resistance Short Circuit Current Sharing Fallacy

topic: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current: Magnetic vs Non-Magnetic Materials

ordered_attempts.stem: A student brings a strong permanent bar magnet near a clean sheet of pure copper. Will the copper sheet be attracted to the magnet?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Yes, copper is strongly attracted because copper is a metal and magnets attract all metals.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-002: Universal Metallic Magnetism Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: Can an electromagnet or permanent bar magnet be used in a scrap yard to separate aluminum cans from iron scrap? Explain why or why not.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Copper is a great conductor of electricity, so it naturally attracts magnetic fields strongly.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-002: Universal Metallic Magnetism Fallacy

topic: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current: Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor in a Magnetic Field

ordered_attempts.stem: A straight wire carrying current is placed inside a uniform magnetic field. Can the magnetic force on the wire ever be in the same direction as the magnetic field lines?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The magnetic force pushes the wire directly along the magnetic field lines towards the North.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-003: Magnetic Force Collinear / Parallel Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A magnetic field points horizontally towards the North. An electric current flows horizontally towards the East. In which direction does the magnetic force act?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Magnetic force always pulls objects in the same direction that the magnetic field is pointing.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-003: Magnetic Force Collinear / Parallel Fallacy

topic: Motion: Describing Motion: Distance and Displacement

ordered_attempts.stem: An athlete completes one round of a circular track of radius 7 m in 40 seconds. What are the total distance covered and the net displacement at the end of the round?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Both distance and displacement are 44 m because distance and displacement are the same thing.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-003: Distance Equals Displacement Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A farmer moves along the boundary of a square field of side 10 m and returns to his starting corner. What is the magnitude of his displacement?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Displacement cannot be zero because the athlete ran hard for 44 meters.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-003: Distance Equals Displacement Fallacy

topic: Motion: Acceleration: Sign of Acceleration and Direction of Motion

ordered_attempts.stem: A car travels towards the West (chosen as negative direction) with velocity -15 m/s and has an acceleration of -3 m/s^2. Is the car speeding up or slowing down?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The car is slowing down because acceleration is negative (-3 m/s^2), and negative acceleration always means braking.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-004: Negative Acceleration Equals Deceleration Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: Does a negative acceleration always mean an object is slowing down? Explain using an example of motion along a chosen coordinate axis.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Negative acceleration is deceleration by definition, so the car must be coming to a stop.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-004: Negative Acceleration Equals Deceleration Fallacy

topic: Motion: Average Speed for Equal Distance Intervals

ordered_attempts.stem: A car travels from town A to town B at an average speed of 60 km/h and returns from B to A along the same route at 40 km/h. What is the average speed for the entire round trip?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Average speed is (60 + 40) / 2 = 50 km/h because you simply take the average of the two numbers.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-005: Average Speed Arithmetic Mean Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A student walks to school at 4 km/h and runs back home along the same path at 6 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole journey.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Average speed = (4 + 6) / 2 = 5 km/h, just add them and divide by 2.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-005: Average Speed Arithmetic Mean Fallacy

topic: Gravitation: Mass and Weight

ordered_attempts.stem: An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg on Earth. What will be the astronaut's mass and weight on the surface of the Moon, where acceleration due to gravity is 1/6th of Earth's (g_moon = 1.63 m/s^2)?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The astronaut's mass on the Moon is 10 kg because mass becomes 1/6th on the Moon (60 / 6 = 10 kg).
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-FOR-003: Mass-Weight Equivalence Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A rock weighs 30 N on Earth. What is its mass on Earth and what will be its mass on the Moon?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Mass drops to 10 kg because there is less gravity to hold the mass together.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-FOR-003: Mass-Weight Equivalence Fallacy

topic: Gravitation: Universal Law of Gravitation (Inverse Square Dependence)

ordered_attempts.stem: The gravitational force between two identical spheres separated by distance r is 100 N. If the distance between their centers is doubled to 2r, what is the new gravitational force?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The new force is 50 N because doubling the distance cuts the gravitational pull in half (100 / 2 = 50 N).
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-GRAV-002: Inverse Square Distance Linearity Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: How does the gravitational force between two planets change if the distance between them is tripled?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Force is inversely proportional to distance, so 2 times the distance means half the force.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-GRAV-002: Inverse Square Distance Linearity Fallacy

topic: Work and Energy: Kinetic Energy and Velocity Dependence

ordered_attempts.stem: A moving automobile of mass 1000 kg has a kinetic energy of 50,000 J at 10 m/s. If its speed is doubled to 20 m/s, what is its new kinetic energy?
ordered_attempts.student_response: New kinetic energy is 100,000 J because doubling speed doubles kinetic energy (2 * 50,000 = 100,000 J).
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ENG-001: Kinetic Energy Velocity Linearity Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: How does the kinetic energy of a moving runner change if their speed increases by a factor of 3?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Kinetic energy is directly proportional to speed, so 2 times speed means 2 times the energy.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ENG-001: Kinetic Energy Velocity Linearity Fallacy

topic: Work and Energy: Work Done by Centripetal / Gravitational Force in Circular Motion

ordered_attempts.stem: A satellite orbits the Earth in a circular path at a constant speed of 7 km/s. What is the total work done by Earth's gravitational force on the satellite in one complete revolution?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Gravity does huge work to keep the satellite moving around the circle for millions of meters.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-WRK-002: Circular Orbit Gravitational Work Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: Does the gravitational force of the Sun do work on the Earth as it moves in its approximately circular orbit?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Work done = F_gravity * 2*pi*r, force times the circumference traveled.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-WRK-002: Circular Orbit Gravitational Work Fallacy

topic: Optics: Half-Lens Remediation

ordered_attempts.stem: Lower half of convex lens covered with black paper. What happens?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Top half of image is missing.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-001: Half-Lens Blocking Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: PhET simulation: Observe virtual mask covering lower half.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Wait, the full image is still formed, just dimmer!
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: COGNITIVE_CONFLICT_RECONCILED: Full image persists with 50% brightness

ordered_attempts.stem: Near-transfer: cover top 30% of lens.
ordered_attempts.student_response: The complete image remains, but brightness is 70%.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: CORRECT: Scientifically Accurate Response

topic: Electricity: Current Conservation Remediation

ordered_attempts.stem: Two identical bulbs in series with 6V battery. Compare ammeters.
ordered_attempts.student_response: A1 = 1.2A, A2 = 0.8A because bulb 1 consumes electric current.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-001: Current Attenuation / Consumption Model

ordered_attempts.stem: PhET Simulation: Observe moving electron dots and ammeters in series.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Both ammeters read identical values (0.90A)! Current is conserved.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: COGNITIVE_CONFLICT_RECONCILED: Current is conserved in closed loop

ordered_attempts.stem: Near-transfer: 100-ohm and 20-ohm resistors in series.
ordered_attempts.student_response: I_in = I_out, because in any series circuit electric charge is conserved.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: CORRECT: Scientifically Accurate Response

topic: Kinematics: Velocity Calculation

ordered_attempts.stem: Runner covers 100 m in 5 s. Speed?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Speed = distance / time = 100 / 5 = 25 m/s (mental arithmetic slip on division).
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: CARELESS_CALCULATION_ERROR

ordered_attempts.stem: Car travels 300 m in 15 s. Speed?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Average speed is distance divided by elapsed time: 300 / 15 = 20 m/s.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: CORRECT: Scientifically Accurate Response

topic: Light – Reflection and Refraction: Image Formation and Aperture of Convex Lens

ordered_attempts.stem: A student forms a sharp image of a lighted candle on a screen using a convex lens of focal length 15 cm. The lower half of the lens is now covered with black paper. What happens to the image on the screen?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The top half of the candle image is completely missing because the bottom half of the lens is covered.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-001: Half-Lens Blocking Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A converging lens of focal length 20 cm projects an image of an illuminated slide. If the upper half of the lens is blocked by an opaque cover, describe the change in the projected image.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Only half the image will appear on the screen because blocking half the glass blocks half the picture.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-001: Half-Lens Blocking Fallacy

topic: Light – Reflection and Refraction: Real Image Formation in Space

ordered_attempts.stem: A convex lens of focal length 15 cm focuses the image of a candle on a white screen placed 40 cm away. If the screen is abruptly removed, does the image still exist in space at that location?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The image disappears completely because an image cannot exist in thin air without a screen to catch it.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-002: Screen Reification (Image Exists Only on Screen)

ordered_attempts.stem: A student forms a sharp real image on a viewing card using a lens of f = 20 cm. When the card is taken away, what happens to the real image?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Without the screen, there is no surface for the image to be drawn on, so no image is formed.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-002: Screen Reification (Image Exists Only on Screen)

topic: Light – Reflection and Refraction: Virtual Images & Mirrors

ordered_attempts.stem: An object is placed at distance 10 cm in front of a flat plane mirror. Do actual light rays pass through the mirror to form the virtual image?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Light rays penetrate through the mirror glass and physically focus 10 cm behind the surface.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-003: Virtual Image Ray Convergence Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: When you see your reflection in a plane mirror at distance 15 cm, what physical process happens behind the mirror glass?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Actual light rays cross each other behind the mirror to create the reflection.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-003: Virtual Image Ray Convergence Fallacy

topic: Light – Reflection and Refraction: New Cartesian Sign Convention and Mirror/Lens Formulae

ordered_attempts.stem: An object is placed at a distance of 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Using the New Cartesian Sign Convention, determine the image distance v.
ordered_attempts.student_response: v = +45.0 cm because distances in real life cannot be negative numbers; I set u = +30 and f = +15.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-004: Sign Convention Spatial Inversion

ordered_attempts.stem: A candle is located 40 cm from a concave mirror with focal length 20 cm. Calculate the image position v using the mirror formula with proper signs.
ordered_attempts.student_response: 1/v = 1/20 - 1/40 giving positive v, because the object is in front of the mirror.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-004: Sign Convention Spatial Inversion

topic: Light – Reflection and Refraction: Refraction through a Rectangular Glass Slab

ordered_attempts.stem: A light ray enters a rectangular glass slab with parallel opposite faces at an angle of incidence of 45°. Describe the direction of the emergent ray relative to the incident ray.
ordered_attempts.student_response: The emergent ray exits bent at a permanent angle because glass bends light permanently like a prism.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-005: Glass Slab Angular Deviation Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: Light passes through a flat rectangular glass block of thickness 15 cm. Does the ray exit permanently bent at an angle or parallel to its original path?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The ray leaves at a sharp angle to its original direction due to refraction at both surfaces.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-005: Glass Slab Angular Deviation Fallacy

topic: The Human Eye and the Colourful World: Defects of Vision and Their Correction

ordered_attempts.stem: A student cannot see distant objects clearly beyond 80 cm but reads a textbook comfortably at 25 cm. Name the defect of vision and specify the type of corrective lens required.
ordered_attempts.student_response: The defect is myopia and must be corrected using a convex lens to converge the light.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-001: Vision Defect Corrective Inversion

ordered_attempts.stem: A person with myopia has a far point of 150 cm. What type of corrective spectacle lens is needed to restore normal distant vision?
ordered_attempts.student_response: A convex spectacles lens is needed because convex lenses help you see things far away.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-001: Vision Defect Corrective Inversion

topic: The Human Eye and the Colourful World: Refraction of Light Through a Prism & Dispersion

ordered_attempts.stem: A narrow beam of white light passes through a triangular glass prism. Which constituent color undergoes the greatest deviation from its original path?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Red light is deviated the most because red has the strongest and most intense color energy.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-002: Prism Dispersion Speed and Deviation Inversion

ordered_attempts.stem: In the dispersion of white light by a glass prism, which color of light travels fastest in glass and which deviates the least?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Red bends at the greatest angle because it has the longest wavelength.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-002: Prism Dispersion Speed and Deviation Inversion

topic: The Human Eye and the Colourful World: Atmospheric Refraction (Twinkling of Stars)

ordered_attempts.stem: Why do stars twinkle at night when viewed from Earth, whereas planets do not twinkle?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Stars twinkle because nuclear explosions on the star surface turn the light on and off rapidly.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-003: Star Twinkling Emission Artifact Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: An observer watches a star on a clear night. What physical process causes the rapid flickering in position and brightness?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Twinkling occurs because thin invisible clouds pass continuously in front of the star.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-003: Star Twinkling Emission Artifact Fallacy

topic: The Human Eye and the Colourful World: Scattering of Light and Colour of the Sky

ordered_attempts.stem: Why does the clear daytime sky appear blue to an observer on the ground?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The sky is blue because it acts as a giant mirror reflecting the blue water of Earth's oceans.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-004: Sky Colour Reflection Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: What physical optical process is responsible for the blue color of the clear sky?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Water vapor droplets in the sky are blue, coloring the atmosphere.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-004: Sky Colour Reflection Fallacy

topic: Electricity: Electric Current in Series Circuits (Conservation of Charge)

ordered_attempts.stem: Two identical bulbs B1 and B2 are connected in series with a 6V battery. An ammeter A1 measures current entering B1, and A2 measures current leaving B2. How do the ammeter readings compare?
ordered_attempts.student_response: A1 > A2 because bulb B1 consumes some of the electric current to glow, leaving less for A2.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-001: Current Attenuation / Consumption Model

ordered_attempts.stem: Three resistors are wired in series. A technician measures current before the first resistor (I1) and after the third resistor (I3). What is the relationship between I1 and I3?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Current decreases along the circuit as it gets used up powering the bulbs.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-001: Current Attenuation / Consumption Model

topic: Electricity: Parallel Circuits and Source Potential Difference

ordered_attempts.stem: A bulb B1 is connected alone across a 12V car battery. An identical bulb B2 is now connected in parallel with B1. How does the brightness of B1 change?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Bulb B1 dims to half brightness because the battery provides a fixed total current that must now be shared.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-002: Battery as Constant Current Source

ordered_attempts.stem: In a domestic parallel household circuit, what happens to the current through a room lamp when a powerful electric heater is switched ON in parallel?
ordered_attempts.student_response: B1 dims because the second bulb steals half the current from the first bulb.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-002: Battery as Constant Current Source

topic: Electricity: Ohm's Law: Voltage, Current, and Resistance Relationship

ordered_attempts.stem: A resistor of 10 ohms is connected to a 6 V battery. Calculate the current through the circuit using Ohm's Law.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Current decreases because the 10 ohm resistor resists and blocks more charge regardless of voltage.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-003: Resistance Reduces Current Independent of Voltage

ordered_attempts.stem: A circuit has a resistance of 20 ohms. The voltage across it is 12 V. What is the current?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The resistor of 20 ohms will definitely reduce the current below 12 A because it opposes flow.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-003: Resistance Reduces Current Independent of Voltage

topic: Electricity: Equivalent Resistance in Parallel Networks

ordered_attempts.stem: Two resistors of 10 ohms and 10 ohms are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance of the network?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The equivalent resistance is 10 + 10 = 100 ohms because adding more resistors always increases total resistance.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-005: Parallel Resistance Addition Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A student adds a second resistor of 20 ohms in parallel across an existing 20 ohm resistor. How does the total circuit resistance change?
ordered_attempts.student_response: R_eq = 400 ohms; resistors always add up linearly regardless of whether they are series or parallel.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-005: Parallel Resistance Addition Fallacy

topic: Electricity: Joule Heating and Electric Power in Parallel vs Series

ordered_attempts.stem: Two electric bulbs rated 60 W and 100 W (both at 220 V) are connected in parallel to a 220 V supply. Which bulb has lower resistance and which glows brighter?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The 20 ohm resistor produces more heat because P = I^2 * R, so higher resistance always means more power dissipated.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-006: Power Formula Mis-selection in Parallel vs Series

ordered_attempts.stem: Two resistors R1 = 5 ohms and R2 = 10 ohms (R1 < R2) are connected in parallel across a constant voltage supply. Which resistor dissipates more heat per second?
ordered_attempts.student_response: By P = I^2 * R, the larger resistor generates more heat because heat is directly proportional to resistance.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-006: Power Formula Mis-selection in Parallel vs Series

topic: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current: Nature of Magnetic Poles vs Electrostatic Charges

ordered_attempts.stem: A stationary electron is placed at rest near the North pole of a strong permanent bar magnet. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force exerted on the electron?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The stationary electron is strongly attracted to the North pole because the North pole is like a positive charge (+Q).
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-001: Magnetic Pole = Electrostatic Charge Equivalence Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: Can a stationary electric charge be attracted or repelled by a static magnetic field from a bar magnet?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The North pole pulls the negative electron inwards by electrostatic attraction.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-001: Magnetic Pole = Electrostatic Charge Equivalence Fallacy

topic: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current: Properties of Magnetic Field Lines

ordered_attempts.stem: Can two magnetic field lines ever cross or intersect each other in space? Explain your reasoning.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Yes, field lines cross each other when two strong magnets are pushed close together.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-004: Field Line Crossing Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A student draws magnetic field lines around two bar magnets and shows two lines crossing at point P. Is this diagram physically valid?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Lines intersect at the neutral point between opposing magnetic poles.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-004: Field Line Crossing Fallacy

topic: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current: Magnetic Force on Current-Carrying Conductor (Fleming's Left Hand Rule)

ordered_attempts.stem: A horizontal wire carries conventional electric current towards the East. A uniform magnetic field is directed towards the North. Using Fleming's Left-Hand Rule, determine the direction of the magnetic force on the wire.
ordered_attempts.student_response: The force is directed vertically Downwards because I used my right hand instead of left hand.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-005: Directional Hand Rule Inversion

ordered_attempts.stem: A proton beam travels horizontally towards the East through a magnetic field pointing North. What is the direction of deflection of the proton beam?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Force points towards the North because magnetic force always pulls objects along the field lines.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-005: Directional Hand Rule Inversion

topic: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current: Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's Law

ordered_attempts.stem: A coil of 100 turns is placed inside a constant steady magnetic field of 2 T. Is any EMF induced in the coil?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Yes, a steady EMF of 100 x 2 = 200 V is induced because the field acts continuously on the coil.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-006: Static Field Induces Constant EMF Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A wire coil with 200 loops sits motionless inside a steady non-changing magnetic field. Does a galvanometer connected to it deflect?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The coil experiences an EMF proportional to field strength times turns = 1000 V.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-006: Static Field Induces Constant EMF Fallacy

topic: Motion: Uniform Motion and Rate of Change of Motion

ordered_attempts.stem: A runner covers a straight track of 100 meters in 5 seconds. Calculate the runner's average speed.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Speed is 500 m/s because I multiplied distance by time (100 * 5 = 500).
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-001: Speed Distance Operation Inversion

ordered_attempts.stem: An automobile travels a distance of 300 m in 15 s along a straight highway. What is its speed?
ordered_attempts.student_response: I calculated speed = 300 * 15 = 4500 m/s.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-001: Speed Distance Operation Inversion

topic: Motion: Acceleration vs Constant Velocity

ordered_attempts.stem: A high-speed train travels along a straight track at a steady, uniform velocity of 20 m/s for 10 seconds. What is the acceleration of the train during this time?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Acceleration is 20 m/s^2 because the train is moving very fast at 20 m/s.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-002: Speed-Acceleration Conflation

ordered_attempts.stem: An aircraft cruises at a constant speed of 50 m/s in a straight line for 5 s. Determine its acceleration.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Acceleration = 50 / 5 = 10 m/s^2 (divided speed by time without checking if speed was changing).
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-002: Speed-Acceleration Conflation

topic: Force and Laws of Motion: Newton's First Law of Motion and Inertia

ordered_attempts.stem: A hockey puck of mass 2 kg glides across perfectly frictionless horizontal ice at a constant speed of 2 m/s. What net horizontal force is required to keep it moving at this speed?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Requires a continuous forward force of 20 N (F = m * v = 2 * 2) to keep it moving.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-FOR-001: Impetus Theory (Force is Required to Sustain Motion)

ordered_attempts.stem: A space probe of mass 5 kg drifts through deep space far from any stars at constant velocity 5 m/s. What forward rocket thrust is needed to maintain its motion?
ordered_attempts.student_response: A forward force of 20 N is needed, because objects stop if no force pushes them.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-FOR-001: Impetus Theory (Force is Required to Sustain Motion)

topic: Force and Laws of Motion: Newton's Third Law (Action and Reaction)

ordered_attempts.stem: A horse pulls a cart forward. By Newton's Third Law, the cart pulls the horse backward with an equal and opposite force. Why doesn't the system remain stationary if the forces are equal and opposite?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The forces cancel out to zero on the cart, so the horse must produce an action force greater than the reaction force to move.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-FOR-002: Action-Reaction Self-Cancellation Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: If every action force produces an equal and opposite reaction force, why do objects ever accelerate instead of canceling out to zero net force?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Third law only applies when objects are stationary; when moving, action becomes greater than reaction.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-FOR-002: Action-Reaction Self-Cancellation Fallacy

topic: Gravitation: Free Fall and Acceleration Due to Gravity (Mass Independence)

ordered_attempts.stem: A heavy cannonball of mass 10 kg and a light feather of mass 10 g are dropped simultaneously from height 20 m inside an evacuated vacuum chamber. Which object reaches the ground first?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The 10 kg cannonball hits first because it is much heavier and gravity pulls it with greater acceleration.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-GRAV-001: Heavier Objects Fall Faster Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: In an Apollo 15 moon experiment without air, an astronaut drops a hammer (1.32 kg) and a falcon feather (0.03 kg) from the same height. Compare their landing times.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Heavier objects fall faster because greater mass means greater downward speed.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-GRAV-001: Heavier Objects Fall Faster Fallacy

topic: Work and Energy: Work Done by Force: Direction Dependence

ordered_attempts.stem: A porter carries a 10 kg bag on his head and walks horizontally for 10 m. How much work is done by the vertical holding force he exerts?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Work done = 10 * 10 = 50 J because force times displacement = work, direction doesn't matter.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-WRK-001: Work Equals Force Times Distance Regardless of Direction

ordered_attempts.stem: A man carries a 20 kg load and walks 20 m on a flat road. Calculate work done by the vertical holding force.
ordered_attempts.student_response: The porter does 160 J of work because he exerts a force of 20 N over 20 m.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-WRK-001: Work Equals Force Times Distance Regardless of Direction

topic: Force and Laws of Motion: Law of Conservation of Momentum

ordered_attempts.stem: A 2 kg ball moving at 2 m/s collides head-on with an identical stationary ball. Ball 1 stops. What is the velocity of ball 2?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Momentum is destroyed when ball 1 stops. Ball 2 receives no velocity since ball 1 has zero momentum at rest.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOM-001: Momentum Not Conserved When Object Stops

ordered_attempts.stem: Ball of mass 3 kg travelling at 3 m/s hits another ball of equal mass at rest and comes to complete stop. Find the speed of second ball.
ordered_attempts.student_response: When ball 1 stops, it loses its momentum. Ball 2 stays stationary.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOM-001: Momentum Not Conserved When Object Stops

topic: Light – Reflection and Refraction: Linear Magnification by Spherical Mirrors and Lenses

ordered_attempts.stem: A spherical mirror produces an image with linear magnification m = -2.0. Is the image enlarged or diminished, and what is its orientation?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The image is diminished and smaller because -2 is a negative number and less than 1.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-006: Magnification Negative Sign Magnitude Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A student computes the magnification of an optical setup as m = -1.5. Describe the size and nature of the image.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Since magnification is negative (-2.0), the image must be smaller than the object.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-006: Magnification Negative Sign Magnitude Fallacy

topic: Light – Reflection and Refraction: Refractive Index and Speed of Light in Media

ordered_attempts.stem: The absolute refractive index of glass is 1.5. Calculate the speed of light in glass given c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s.
ordered_attempts.student_response: v = c * n = 3.0e8 * 1.5 = 4.5e8 m/s; light speeds up because glass has higher index 1.5.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-007: Refractive Index Speed Proportionality Inversion

ordered_attempts.stem: Medium A has refractive index 1.33 and Medium B has refractive index 1.65. In which medium does light travel faster?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Light travels faster in medium B (n=1.65) because greater refractive index accelerates the light rays.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-007: Refractive Index Speed Proportionality Inversion

topic: Light – Reflection and Refraction: Image Formation by Concave (Diverging) Lenses

ordered_attempts.stem: A student places an illuminated object 50 cm in front of a concave lens of focal length 20 cm. Can a sharp image be formed on a screen placed on the other side?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Yes, if the object is placed beyond 2F (at 50 cm), a real inverted image will be formed on the screen.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-008: Concave Lens Real Image Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: Under what object distance conditions can a concave (diverging) spherical lens form a real inverted image?
ordered_attempts.student_response: A real image forms on the screen as long as the screen is positioned at the focal distance 20 cm.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-008: Concave Lens Real Image Fallacy

topic: The Human Eye and the Colourful World: Colour of the Sun at Sunrise and Sunset

ordered_attempts.stem: Why does the Sun appear reddish during sunrise and sunset, whereas it appears white at noon?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The Sun looks red at sunset because it cools down at the end of the day, lowering its temperature.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-005: Sunset Red Absorption / Temperature Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: What optical phenomenon causes the reddish appearance of the Sun near the horizon?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Red appearance happens because evening clouds absorb all red light and reflect it down.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-005: Sunset Red Absorption / Temperature Fallacy

topic: The Human Eye and the Colourful World: Atmospheric Refraction (Advanced Sunrise and Delayed Sunset)

ordered_attempts.stem: Why is the Sun visible to an observer on Earth about 2 minutes before the actual sunrise and 2 minutes after actual sunset?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The Sun is visible early because light travels in straight lines and the Earth rotates faster in the morning.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-006: Horizon Straight-Line Geometric Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: What causes the apparent daily lengthening of daylight time by approximately 4 minutes?
ordered_attempts.student_response: We see the Sun early because clouds act as mirrors and reflect the Sun over the curvature.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-006: Horizon Straight-Line Geometric Fallacy

topic: Electricity: Electric Potential Difference vs Electric Current

ordered_attempts.stem: A student says: 'In this circuit, 12 volts of electricity is flowing through the 4-ohm resistor.' What conceptual error has the student made?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Voltage flows through the resistor and gets consumed just like water pressure flows through a pipe.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-004: Voltage-Current Conflation / Voltage as Flowing Entity

ordered_attempts.stem: Explain the fundamental operational difference between electric current and potential difference in a circuit.
ordered_attempts.student_response: There is no error; voltage and current are two names for the same flowing electricity.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-004: Voltage-Current Conflation / Voltage as Flowing Entity

topic: Electricity: Factors on which the Resistance of a Conductor Depends (Resistivity)

ordered_attempts.stem: A cylindrical copper wire of resistance R and resistivity rho is cut into two equal halves. What are the resistance and resistivity of each half?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Both resistance and resistivity are halved (R' = R/2 and rho' = rho/2) because cutting the wire cuts everything in half.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-007: Resistivity Dimensional Dependence Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A wire of length L and uniform cross-section A has resistivity rho. If the wire is stretched to double its length, how does its resistivity change?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Resistivity doubles when length doubles because rho = R * A / L.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-007: Resistivity Dimensional Dependence Fallacy

topic: Electricity: Short Circuit and Parallel Branch Current Distribution

ordered_attempts.stem: A lighted bulb is connected to a battery. A thick copper wire of negligible resistance is now connected directly across the two terminals of the bulb. What happens to the bulb?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The bulb stays on at half brightness because parallel branches always split the current equally.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-008: Zero-Resistance Short Circuit Current Sharing Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: In a circuit with a bulb glowing brightly, an ideal conducting wire (R = 0) is connected in parallel with the bulb. Does the bulb remain lit?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The bulb glows brighter because adding an extra wire provides an easier path for energy to reach it.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-008: Zero-Resistance Short Circuit Current Sharing Fallacy

topic: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current: Magnetic vs Non-Magnetic Materials

ordered_attempts.stem: A student brings a strong permanent bar magnet near a clean sheet of pure copper. Will the copper sheet be attracted to the magnet?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Yes, copper is strongly attracted because copper is a metal and magnets attract all metals.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-002: Universal Metallic Magnetism Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: Can an electromagnet or permanent bar magnet be used in a scrap yard to separate aluminum cans from iron scrap? Explain why or why not.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Copper is a great conductor of electricity, so it naturally attracts magnetic fields strongly.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-002: Universal Metallic Magnetism Fallacy

topic: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current: Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor in a Magnetic Field

ordered_attempts.stem: A straight wire carrying current is placed inside a uniform magnetic field. Can the magnetic force on the wire ever be in the same direction as the magnetic field lines?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The magnetic force pushes the wire directly along the magnetic field lines towards the North.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-003: Magnetic Force Collinear / Parallel Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A magnetic field points horizontally towards the North. An electric current flows horizontally towards the East. In which direction does the magnetic force act?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Magnetic force always pulls objects in the same direction that the magnetic field is pointing.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-003: Magnetic Force Collinear / Parallel Fallacy

topic: Motion: Describing Motion: Distance and Displacement

ordered_attempts.stem: An athlete completes one round of a circular track of radius 7 m in 40 seconds. What are the total distance covered and the net displacement at the end of the round?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Both distance and displacement are 44 m because distance and displacement are the same thing.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-003: Distance Equals Displacement Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A farmer moves along the boundary of a square field of side 10 m and returns to his starting corner. What is the magnitude of his displacement?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Displacement cannot be zero because the athlete ran hard for 44 meters.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-003: Distance Equals Displacement Fallacy

topic: Motion: Acceleration: Sign of Acceleration and Direction of Motion

ordered_attempts.stem: A car travels towards the West (chosen as negative direction) with velocity -15 m/s and has an acceleration of -3 m/s^2. Is the car speeding up or slowing down?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The car is slowing down because acceleration is negative (-3 m/s^2), and negative acceleration always means braking.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-004: Negative Acceleration Equals Deceleration Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: Does a negative acceleration always mean an object is slowing down? Explain using an example of motion along a chosen coordinate axis.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Negative acceleration is deceleration by definition, so the car must be coming to a stop.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-004: Negative Acceleration Equals Deceleration Fallacy

topic: Motion: Average Speed for Equal Distance Intervals

ordered_attempts.stem: A car travels from town A to town B at an average speed of 60 km/h and returns from B to A along the same route at 40 km/h. What is the average speed for the entire round trip?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Average speed is (60 + 40) / 2 = 50 km/h because you simply take the average of the two numbers.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-005: Average Speed Arithmetic Mean Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A student walks to school at 4 km/h and runs back home along the same path at 6 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole journey.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Average speed = (4 + 6) / 2 = 5 km/h, just add them and divide by 2.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-005: Average Speed Arithmetic Mean Fallacy

topic: Gravitation: Mass and Weight

ordered_attempts.stem: An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg on Earth. What will be the astronaut's mass and weight on the surface of the Moon, where acceleration due to gravity is 1/6th of Earth's (g_moon = 1.63 m/s^2)?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The astronaut's mass on the Moon is 10 kg because mass becomes 1/6th on the Moon (60 / 6 = 10 kg).
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-FOR-003: Mass-Weight Equivalence Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A rock weighs 30 N on Earth. What is its mass on Earth and what will be its mass on the Moon?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Mass drops to 10 kg because there is less gravity to hold the mass together.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-FOR-003: Mass-Weight Equivalence Fallacy

topic: Gravitation: Universal Law of Gravitation (Inverse Square Dependence)

ordered_attempts.stem: The gravitational force between two identical spheres separated by distance r is 100 N. If the distance between their centers is doubled to 2r, what is the new gravitational force?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The new force is 50 N because doubling the distance cuts the gravitational pull in half (100 / 2 = 50 N).
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-GRAV-002: Inverse Square Distance Linearity Fallacy

ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-GRAV-002: Inverse Square Distance Linearity Fallacy

topic: Work and Energy: Kinetic Energy and Velocity Dependence

ordered_attempts.stem: A moving automobile of mass 1000 kg has a kinetic energy of 50,000 J at 10 m/s. If its speed is doubled to 20 m/s, what is its new kinetic energy?
ordered_attempts.student_response: New kinetic energy is 100,000 J because doubling speed doubles kinetic energy (2 * 50,000 = 100,000 J).
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ENG-001: Kinetic Energy Velocity Linearity Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: How does the kinetic energy of a moving runner change if their speed increases by a factor of 3?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Kinetic energy is directly proportional to speed, so 2 times speed means 2 times the energy.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ENG-001: Kinetic Energy Velocity Linearity Fallacy

topic: Work and Energy: Work Done by Centripetal / Gravitational Force in Circular Motion

ordered_attempts.stem: A satellite orbits the Earth in a circular path at a constant speed of 7 km/s. What is the total work done by Earth's gravitational force on the satellite in one complete revolution?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Gravity does huge work to keep the satellite moving around the circle for millions of meters.

ordered_attempts.student_response: Work done = F_gravity * 2*pi*r, force times the circumference traveled.

topic: Optics: Half-Lens Remediation

topic: Kinematics: Velocity Calculation

ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: CORRECT: Scientifically Accurate Response

topic: Light – Reflection and Refraction: Image Formation and Aperture of Convex Lens

ordered_attempts.stem: A student forms a sharp image of a lighted candle on a screen using a convex lens of focal length 15 cm. The lower half of the lens is now covered with black paper. What happens to the image on the screen?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The top half of the candle image is completely missing because the bottom half of the lens is covered.

ordered_attempts.stem: A converging lens of focal length 20 cm projects an image of an illuminated slide. If the upper half of the lens is blocked by an opaque cover, describe the change in the projected image.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Only half the image will appear on the screen because blocking half the glass blocks half the picture.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-001: Half-Lens Blocking Fallacy

topic: Light – Reflection and Refraction: Real Image Formation in Space

ordered_attempts.stem: A convex lens of focal length 15 cm focuses the image of a candle on a white screen placed 40 cm away. If the screen is abruptly removed, does the image still exist in space at that location?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The image disappears completely because an image cannot exist in thin air without a screen to catch it.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-002: Screen Reification (Image Exists Only on Screen)

ordered_attempts.stem: A student forms a sharp real image on a viewing card using a lens of f = 20 cm. When the card is taken away, what happens to the real image?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Without the screen, there is no surface for the image to be drawn on, so no image is formed.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-002: Screen Reification (Image Exists Only on Screen)

topic: Light – Reflection and Refraction: Virtual Images & Mirrors

ordered_attempts.stem: An object is placed at distance 10 cm in front of a flat plane mirror. Do actual light rays pass through the mirror to form the virtual image?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Light rays penetrate through the mirror glass and physically focus 10 cm behind the surface.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-003: Virtual Image Ray Convergence Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: When you see your reflection in a plane mirror at distance 15 cm, what physical process happens behind the mirror glass?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Actual light rays cross each other behind the mirror to create the reflection.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-003: Virtual Image Ray Convergence Fallacy

topic: Light – Reflection and Refraction: New Cartesian Sign Convention and Mirror/Lens Formulae

ordered_attempts.stem: An object is placed at a distance of 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Using the New Cartesian Sign Convention, determine the image distance v.
ordered_attempts.student_response: v = +45.0 cm because distances in real life cannot be negative numbers; I set u = +30 and f = +15.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-004: Sign Convention Spatial Inversion

ordered_attempts.stem: A candle is located 40 cm from a concave mirror with focal length 20 cm. Calculate the image position v using the mirror formula with proper signs.
ordered_attempts.student_response: 1/v = 1/20 - 1/40 giving positive v, because the object is in front of the mirror.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-004: Sign Convention Spatial Inversion

topic: Light – Reflection and Refraction: Refraction through a Rectangular Glass Slab

ordered_attempts.stem: A light ray enters a rectangular glass slab with parallel opposite faces at an angle of incidence of 45°. Describe the direction of the emergent ray relative to the incident ray.
ordered_attempts.student_response: The emergent ray exits bent at a permanent angle because glass bends light permanently like a prism.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-005: Glass Slab Angular Deviation Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: Light passes through a flat rectangular glass block of thickness 15 cm. Does the ray exit permanently bent at an angle or parallel to its original path?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The ray leaves at a sharp angle to its original direction due to refraction at both surfaces.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-OPT-005: Glass Slab Angular Deviation Fallacy

topic: The Human Eye and the Colourful World: Defects of Vision and Their Correction

ordered_attempts.stem: A student cannot see distant objects clearly beyond 80 cm but reads a textbook comfortably at 25 cm. Name the defect of vision and specify the type of corrective lens required.
ordered_attempts.student_response: The defect is myopia and must be corrected using a convex lens to converge the light.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-001: Vision Defect Corrective Inversion

ordered_attempts.stem: A person with myopia has a far point of 150 cm. What type of corrective spectacle lens is needed to restore normal distant vision?
ordered_attempts.student_response: A convex spectacles lens is needed because convex lenses help you see things far away.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-001: Vision Defect Corrective Inversion

topic: The Human Eye and the Colourful World: Refraction of Light Through a Prism & Dispersion

ordered_attempts.stem: A narrow beam of white light passes through a triangular glass prism. Which constituent color undergoes the greatest deviation from its original path?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Red light is deviated the most because red has the strongest and most intense color energy.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-002: Prism Dispersion Speed and Deviation Inversion

ordered_attempts.stem: In the dispersion of white light by a glass prism, which color of light travels fastest in glass and which deviates the least?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Red bends at the greatest angle because it has the longest wavelength.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-002: Prism Dispersion Speed and Deviation Inversion

topic: The Human Eye and the Colourful World: Atmospheric Refraction (Twinkling of Stars)

ordered_attempts.stem: Why do stars twinkle at night when viewed from Earth, whereas planets do not twinkle?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Stars twinkle because nuclear explosions on the star surface turn the light on and off rapidly.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-003: Star Twinkling Emission Artifact Fallacy

ordered_attempts.student_response: Twinkling occurs because thin invisible clouds pass continuously in front of the star.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-003: Star Twinkling Emission Artifact Fallacy

topic: The Human Eye and the Colourful World: Scattering of Light and Colour of the Sky

ordered_attempts.stem: Why does the clear daytime sky appear blue to an observer on the ground?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The sky is blue because it acts as a giant mirror reflecting the blue water of Earth's oceans.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-004: Sky Colour Reflection Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: What physical optical process is responsible for the blue color of the clear sky?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Water vapor droplets in the sky are blue, coloring the atmosphere.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-EYE-004: Sky Colour Reflection Fallacy

topic: Electricity: Electric Current in Series Circuits (Conservation of Charge)

ordered_attempts.stem: Two identical bulbs B1 and B2 are connected in series with a 6V battery. An ammeter A1 measures current entering B1, and A2 measures current leaving B2. How do the ammeter readings compare?
ordered_attempts.student_response: A1 > A2 because bulb B1 consumes some of the electric current to glow, leaving less for A2.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-001: Current Attenuation / Consumption Model

ordered_attempts.stem: Three resistors are wired in series. A technician measures current before the first resistor (I1) and after the third resistor (I3). What is the relationship between I1 and I3?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Current decreases along the circuit as it gets used up powering the bulbs.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-001: Current Attenuation / Consumption Model

topic: Electricity: Parallel Circuits and Source Potential Difference

ordered_attempts.stem: A bulb B1 is connected alone across a 12V car battery. An identical bulb B2 is now connected in parallel with B1. How does the brightness of B1 change?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Bulb B1 dims to half brightness because the battery provides a fixed total current that must now be shared.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-002: Battery as Constant Current Source

ordered_attempts.stem: In a domestic parallel household circuit, what happens to the current through a room lamp when a powerful electric heater is switched ON in parallel?
ordered_attempts.student_response: B1 dims because the second bulb steals half the current from the first bulb.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-002: Battery as Constant Current Source

topic: Electricity: Ohm's Law: Voltage, Current, and Resistance Relationship

ordered_attempts.stem: A resistor of 10 ohms is connected to a 6 V battery. Calculate the current through the circuit using Ohm's Law.
ordered_attempts.student_response: Current decreases because the 10 ohm resistor resists and blocks more charge regardless of voltage.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-003: Resistance Reduces Current Independent of Voltage

ordered_attempts.stem: A circuit has a resistance of 20 ohms. The voltage across it is 12 V. What is the current?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The resistor of 20 ohms will definitely reduce the current below 12 A because it opposes flow.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-003: Resistance Reduces Current Independent of Voltage

topic: Electricity: Equivalent Resistance in Parallel Networks

ordered_attempts.stem: Two resistors of 10 ohms and 10 ohms are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance of the network?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The equivalent resistance is 10 + 10 = 100 ohms because adding more resistors always increases total resistance.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-005: Parallel Resistance Addition Fallacy

ordered_attempts.stem: A student adds a second resistor of 20 ohms in parallel across an existing 20 ohm resistor. How does the total circuit resistance change?
ordered_attempts.student_response: R_eq = 400 ohms; resistors always add up linearly regardless of whether they are series or parallel.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-005: Parallel Resistance Addition Fallacy

topic: Electricity: Joule Heating and Electric Power in Parallel vs Series

ordered_attempts.stem: Two electric bulbs rated 60 W and 100 W (both at 220 V) are connected in parallel to a 220 V supply. Which bulb has lower resistance and which glows brighter?
ordered_attempts.student_response: The 20 ohm resistor produces more heat because P = I^2 * R, so higher resistance always means more power dissipated.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-006: Power Formula Mis-selection in Parallel vs Series

ordered_attempts.stem: Two resistors R1 = 5 ohms and R2 = 10 ohms (R1 < R2) are connected in parallel across a constant voltage supply. Which resistor dissipates more heat per second?
ordered_attempts.student_response: By P = I^2 * R, the larger resistor generates more heat because heat is directly proportional to resistance.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-ELEC-006: Power Formula Mis-selection in Parallel vs Series

topic: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current: Nature of Magnetic Poles vs Electrostatic Charges

ordered_attempts.stem: A stationary electron is placed at rest near the North pole of a strong permanent bar magnet. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force exerted on the electron?

ordered_attempts.student_response: The North pole pulls the negative electron inwards by electrostatic attraction.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-001: Magnetic Pole = Electrostatic Charge Equivalence Fallacy

topic: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current: Properties of Magnetic Field Lines

ordered_attempts.stem: Can two magnetic field lines ever cross or intersect each other in space? Explain your reasoning.

ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-004: Field Line Crossing Fallacy

ordered_attempts.student_response: Lines intersect at the neutral point between opposing magnetic poles.

topic: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current: Magnetic Force on Current-Carrying Conductor (Fleming's Left Hand Rule)

ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-005: Directional Hand Rule Inversion

topic: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current: Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's Law

ordered_attempts.stem: A coil of 100 turns is placed inside a constant steady magnetic field of 2 T. Is any EMF induced in the coil?

ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MAG-006: Static Field Induces Constant EMF Fallacy

topic: Motion: Uniform Motion and Rate of Change of Motion

ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-001: Speed Distance Operation Inversion

topic: Motion: Acceleration vs Constant Velocity

ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-MOT-002: Speed-Acceleration Conflation

topic: Force and Laws of Motion: Newton's First Law of Motion and Inertia

ordered_attempts.stem: A hockey puck of mass 2 kg glides across perfectly frictionless horizontal ice at a constant speed of 2 m/s. What net horizontal force is required to keep it moving at this speed?
ordered_attempts.student_response: Requires a continuous forward force of 20 N (F = m * v = 2 * 2) to keep it moving.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-FOR-001: Impetus Theory (Force is Required to Sustain Motion)

ordered_attempts.stem: A space probe of mass 5 kg drifts through deep space far from any stars at constant velocity 5 m/s. What forward rocket thrust is needed to maintain its motion?
ordered_attempts.student_response: A forward force of 20 N is needed, because objects stop if no force pushes them.
ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-FOR-001: Impetus Theory (Force is Required to Sustain Motion)

topic: Force and Laws of Motion: Newton's Third Law (Action and Reaction)

ordered_attempts.individual_diagnosis: MISC-FOR-002: Action-Reaction Self-Cancellation Fallacy
